reason: Tall is the height of the whole plant (liane, herb, tree). The examples are correct.
Stipules are often lanceolate-triangular, and the examples show that.
The orchid rostellum can be triangular. The examples are correct.

The examples are plain mm values, and some are for the free part ('free to 0.3 mm'). They could be hypanthium length, depth or the free lobes. A rule would need the source word (long, deep, high) and whether it is the free part.
Pinnules can be stalked, sessile or stipitate, which is how they attach to the pinna.
Pyrene surfaces are rugose or pitted, and the examples fit. Some examples say 'abaxially', which suggests leaves. Check that the bearer is the pyrene.
The scutellum has a length in mm, and the examples are correct.
A leaf blade can be concave, on the adaxial side or near the apex.
A midvein is often grooved or channeled on one face.
Size is the attribute for pinnae. The examples compare size with the adjacent pair, which is meaningful here.
Filiform corolla lobes or tubes are possible. Some examples are about laminae or plicae, which are other parts. A rule would need the real bearer (tube, lobe, corolla) in the statement.
'characteristic' is the root PATO class and is too general. 'Simple or forked' is a branching quality, so use a branching or simple/forked term instead.
The palea is shorter than the lemma, or short. This is meaningful and the examples are correct.
A stalk or stipe can be short. The examples are correct.
A corolla lip can be obovate. The examples are correct, although a few say 'middle lobe', which is another part.
A leaf base can be tapered or narrowed, and the examples are correct.
A bract margin can be entire. The examples are correct.
Leaf teeth have a 2-D shape (ovate, oblong). The examples are correct.
Anthers can be shorter than the filaments, and the examples are correct.
Wrong part. The examples are about a 'spur' (a floral spur), which was read as short shoot. The spur is not a short shoot.
The examples are the crenate margin of a lobe. PATO 'scalloped' is the crenate reading and the pair is meaningful. The margin is the more exact bearer.
A pericarp can be woody. The examples are correct.
Spores can be spherical. The example 'globules' is a different thing but does not change the pair.

Wrong part. The examples (lanceolate, ovate, French 'allongées') describe leaves or bracts, not trichomes of the shoot axis. Shape of a trichome is meaningful only when the trichome is the real subject.
'characteristic' is the root PATO class and is too general. 'Entire or dentate' is about the margin, which is a different part, so use a margin quality on the margin.
Bracts, or parts of them such as the apex, can be flat. The examples are correct.
'Ellipsoid' is the prolate shape of a capsule. The examples are correct.
A connective can be truncated, and the examples are correct.
A pollinarium (pollinium) has a length in mm. The examples are correct.
Pinnules are alternate or opposite on the pinna. The pinnule is a fair bearer for this arrangement.
A leaflet can be dissected or divided. The examples are correct.
A capsule can be straight (versus curved). The examples are correct.
A leaf sheath can be striate (grass and sedge sheaths). The examples are correct.
An indusium can be small. The examples are correct.
Fronds can be papery in texture. The examples are correct.
A leaf rachis can be glabrous. The examples are correct.
A calyptra has a length in mm. One example ('as long as hypanthium') is a comparison, but the pair is fine.
A pale or pallid leaflet face is a low-saturation colour. The examples are correct, and the abaxial side stays in the statement.
Lips and lobes can spread. The examples are correct, though some say 'lateral lobes' or 'mid-lobe', which are other parts.
A whole plant can be ephemeral or short-lived. The examples are correct.
'structure' is a very general PATO term. The examples say confluent or coalescing, which is a fusion quality, so use a fused or confluent term.
A branch can be velvety with hairs. One example ('bordered by poorly defined velvety zone') looks like a different part, but the pair is fine.
A labellum lobe has a 2-D shape (ovate, oblong, cuneate-flabellate). The examples are correct.
An indusium can be reniform, which is typical for ferns. The examples are correct.
A stigma can be square, though this is rare. The examples are correct.
A moss alar cell has a length. The examples are length × width in µm, so the width should be kept as a separate quality.
A flower bud can be ovoid or obovoid, and the examples are correct.
The examples are the serrate margin of a lobe. The pair is meaningful, and the margin is the more exact bearer.
A pseudobulb has a colour such as green or purple. The examples are correct.
Boat-shaped (navicular, cymbiform) bracts are scaphoid. The examples are correct.
An awn can be twisted or contorted. The examples are correct.
A stem node can be prominent. The examples are correct.
A pedicel can be ciliate. The examples are correct, though some ciliate margins belong to other parts.
A corolla lip can be glabrous. The examples are correct, and the surface side stays in the statement.
Perigynia are ascending or spreading, and the examples are correct.
'Subsessile' and 'stipitate' are about the frond or its stipe, which is fine. 'Coherent in groups' is a different thing (sori or pinnae). A rule would need to keep only the sessile/stalked wording.
A corolla lip can have an emarginate apex. The examples are correct.
A leaf can be floccose, meaning it has cottony hairs. The examples describe the cottony hairs on the leaf.
Veinlets can be raised on a face of the leaf. The examples are correct.
Fronds can be leathery. The examples are correct.
